newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends softer vs most major currencies in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends softer vs most major currencies in U.S..

text.p: *Dollar ends weaker vs mark, yen, Swissy and sterling.
*Fresh concern Italy may not qualify for first round of EMU in Jan 1999 helped bolster mark vs some European units and dollar.
*Two-day FOMC confab starts Tues. Any announcement seen Weds.
*25 of 26 analysts in Reuter poll see Fed keeping rates steady
*US new home sales due Tues 1000 EST. Dec seen at 745,000.

The dollar ended weaker as fresh concern that Italy may not qualify for the first group to be included in European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) planned for January 1, 1999 boosted the mark, experts said.
The mark racked up gains against several currencies, including the Italian lira, Spanish peseta and the greenback.

Horst Siebert, an economic advisor to the German government, was quoted in an Italian newspaper questioning whether Italy could fulfill requirements for joining the single European currency in 1999 without "window dressing" its accounts.
Siebert also said that Germans feared that Italy's participation in the single currency would bring instability to the project.

"What happened is people tend to try to buy the mark against those currencies when there is doubt about their entry into the EMU," said Thomas Arnold, a vice president and chief dealer of foreign exchange at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.
"So, what happens in the dollar market is...people are trying to sell dollars against the mark," Arnold said.
The dollar closed at 1.6396/01 marks and 121.65/75 yen, down from 1.6480/85 marks and 122.13/23 yen at the open.
In late New York dealings, the mark traded around 988.45/85 lire and 85.20/22 pesetas, up from about 986.50/85 lire and 84.87/90 pesetas in very early trading.
The dollar had hit an intraday high of 1.6490 marks and 122.24 yen just as trading got underway in New York following overnight remarks by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Hashimoto told a parliamentary committee on Monday that the dollar is unlikely to be lowered through international cooperation, even though excessive strengthening of the currency was undesirable.
"It helped the dollar," said Diego Giurleo, vice president of Treasury at Royal Bank of Canada.
"He's basically saying there is going to be no concerted intervention to bring the dollar down," Giurleo added.
Since hitting post-World War II lows of 1.3438 marks on March 8, 1995 and 79.75 yen on April 19, 1995, the dollar has risen 24 percent versus the mark and more than 50 percent on the yen.
Senior financial officials of the Group of Seven major industrial powers helped to engineer the sharp dollar gains after the currency hit bottom in 1995.
Therefore, currency traders are keenly searching for any clues about whether these officials will decide the dollar rally has gone far enough when they meet again in Berlin next Saturday.
On Tuesday and Wednesday, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the Federal Reserve's policy arm, meets to decide the future course of U.S. short-term interest rates.

Most analysts predicted policy makers will leave rates unchanged. The last time the FOMC altered rates was on January 31, 1996, when it cut two key short-term rates in a bid to stimulate economic growth.
Any FOMC announcement on rates is expected on
Wednesday.
Expectations are for unchanged monetary policy, said Bob Lynch, a senior currency analyst at MMS International.
"You may see some tail off in activity just in case the Fed surprises (the market) with a move," Lynch added.
Elsewhere, the dollar ended at 1.4182/92 Swiss francs, down from 1.4315/25 francs at the open. Sterling rose to $1.6195/05 from $1.6122/32 at the open.
The dollar ended at Canadian $1.3443/48, just shy of C$1.3444/49. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7653/58 from $0.7679/84 at the open. -- D. Sells, 212-859-1668
